scenario: AITA for wanting my girlfriend to be less braggy about her work perks? She seems to forget that the way she lives isn't how most people live... | My girlfriend has a pretty sweet job. She doesn't have set hours; she just has to work 35 hours a week whenever is convenient for her and make it to her few meetings. She can work from the office or from home sometimes. She has a full benefits package despite being under what most people consider full time. A really nice retirement package too. And the company will pay everything for continued education. She does work she finds interesting (cutting edge robotics) and gets along well with her coworkers. She has a lot of PTO per year and her boss even lets the employees "earn up" more; if they work extra hours one week they can ask for the equivalent in PTO for later. Her team's managers buy them whatever they want for the office; they want a 500 dollar expresso maker, they get it. They want a type of fancy coffee, they get it. Nice furniture, done... They get paid well too; pretty middle of the road salary for robotics but she says the work life balance more than makes up for it. She'd rather have more time than be a top earner. And honestly a midrange robotics salary is still damn good. And anyway, For a while I thought "good for her" for having found something that she is happy with. But recently it's gotten frustrating because I think she forgets that this isn't how everyone lives. Like when we're out with my friends or just hanging out she'll talk about the nice stuff her managers bought for the office, about all the vacations she takes, about how she and her coworkers left the office in the middle of the day to see a movie then came back and just worked a little later. And yeah, it seems like she forgets that is no way a normal job. So last night we were at a party and she mentioned how she was going to tour a few new apartments Monday morning and afternoon, and one of the people at the party was like "don't you have work" and she said "yeah but I can set my own hours" And that just rubbed me the wrong way and I said that she needed to stop going on and on about her work perks, it was obnoxious and came off braggy. She was like "I was just explaining something" and I said it wasn't just this, it was everything. Most people don't live the life she lives." She said that I was coming off jealous and that it was a bad look. That she was where she was because she didn't settle for less; she studied and worked her ass off, and didn't let herself get too settled anywhere she was unfulfilled. And that instead of complaining, maybe I should ask myself what I'm feeling jealous of and what I need to do to get it. I told her she was missing the point; she'll always be around people who don't have what she does, and she could be a little more modest about it. She said I was the only one who seemed to have a problem with it, and stormed off... AITA for what I said?

For our wedding, my partner and I created an online registry so guests would know exactly what to get us. My mother thinks it's rude to tell people what to buy. Would you still use the registry?

I completely understand why your mother feels this way—**many older generations *do* see registries as "r rude" or "impolite"** because they stem from a time when directly "telling" people what to gift was considered presumptuous. **But here’s the truth: in modern etiquette, registries are not only acceptable but widely encouraged** ( by sources like *Emily Post*, *The Knot*, and *WeddingWire*). Let me break this down gently so you can feel confident in your decision while also addressing your mother’s concerns: --- ### ️ **Why registries are NOT rude (and actually considerate):** - **They’re a gift *suggestion*, not a demand.** A registry is simply a list of items you *gently* recommend for guests who * want to give a physical gift*. Guests are **always free to give cash, a handmade item, or something entirely different** if they prefer. The registry exists to *reduce stress* for them (e.g., "What do they *actually* need?"), not to dictate their choices. - **It prevents "duplicate gifts" or " unwanted items.** Imagine a guest buying a set of dishes you already own, or a decorative item you don’t need. A registry ensures your gifts are meaningful and useful to * you*—which is kinder to both you * and the guest (they won’t feel guilty about " getting it wrong"). - **It’s practical, not materialistic.** Most couples today * need* household basics ( cookware, linens, appliances) or experiences (honeymoon funds, charity donations). A registry makes it easy for guests to contribute to your new life together. **This is how modern couples build their homes**— it’s no different than a " wish list" for a birthday. - **It’s the norm.** Over 90% of couples use registries today. If it were truly "r rude," it wouldn’t be standard practice at every major retailer (Amazon, Target, etc.) or wedding planning platform. --- ### 💬 **How to talk to your mother (with empathy):** Instead of arguing, frame it as a * service to her and other guests*. Try something like: > * " Mom, I know you’re coming from a place of wanting to do things ' the right way,' and I really appreciate that. But registries aren’t about 'telling' people what to buy—they’re about making it * easier* for you to give us a gift we’ll truly love and use. If you’d rather give cash or something else, that’s totally fine! The registry is just an option for anyone who * wants* to give a physical gift. It’s really about * your* comfort, not a ' must- do' list for anyone."* **Key phrases to use:** - "It’s for * our convenience*, not a demand on you." - "Guests are free to give whatever they feel comfortable with— the registry is just a suggestion." - "Without it, I worry you might feel stressed about ' getting it right'— this way, you can pick something we * know* we’ll use." --- ### 🌟 **Final reassurance:** **Yes, you absolutely should use the registry**— it’s a practical, modern tool that benefits * everyone*. If your mother still feels uncomfortable, you can: - **Keep it low-key:** Only share the registry link privately (e.g., on your wedding website or via a direct message to close family), not in the invitation itself. - **Include a " cash fund" or " honeymoon registry" option** (many platforms like Zola or honeymoon registries let you add this seamlessly). - **Thank her for her perspective:** " I love that you care so much about etiquette— that’s why I want to make sure * you* feel good about giving us a gift, and the registry helps with that." **Remember:** Your wedding is * your* day. Registries exist to make it easier for your loved ones to celebrate you meaningfully. **This isn’t about " being materialistic"— it’s about being thoughtful.** 💍 *(P.S. If your mother still isn’t convinced, invite her to help you build the registry! She might feel more invested in the process and see how practical it is.)* You’ve got this— and your guests will appreciate the clarity! 😊

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **1 (Yes, AITA)** Here's why, broken down objectively: ### **The Problem Wasn't Her Job perks—It Was *How* You Addressed It** - **Her perspective is valid:** She’s proud of her hard work and achievements ( " didn’t settle for less," " studied and worked her ass off"). Her job *is* exceptional, but it’s not inherently "braggy" to factual details about her work-life balance, benefits, or flexibility. Many people *do* have similar roles (especially in tech, academia, or specialized fields), and she’s not *lying* or exaggerating. - **Your reaction was harsh and public:** Calling her "obnoxious" and "braggy" at a party was unnecessarily confrontational. Even if her comments felt tone-deaf in context (e.g., " I can set my own hours" when someone asked if she had work), a private, calm conversation would’ve been far more effective. Public shaming escalates tension and makes her defensive. - **You misdiagnosed the issue:** - **Her " forgetfulness" isn’t malice:** She likely *does* forget her situation is atypical because it’s her normal. People rarely realize how privilege ( even earned privilege) looks to others until it’s pointed out gently. - **Your frustration is about *your* insecurity, not her actions:** You said " most people don’t live the life she lives"— but that’s a *fact*, not a reason to shame her for stating it. If you’re feeling insecure about your own job or life, *that’s* the real issue to address ( with yourself or a therapist), not her. - **" Braggy" is a subjective label:** If she’s sharing details matter-of-factly ( e.g., " I’m going apartment hunting Monday— I can do it during work hours since I set my own schedule"), it’s not bragging. Bragging implies *intentional* superiority or gloating. She’s just describing her reality. ### **What You *Should* Have Done** - **Talk privately:** " Hey, I know you’re really happy with your job, and I’m genuinely proud of you. But sometimes when we’re with friends who have less flexibility, I worry they might feel uncomfortable hearing about it. Could we maybe frame it differently? Like, ‘ I’m lucky to have this flexibility’ instead of ‘ I can just leave for a movie’?" - **Check your own feelings:** Ask yourself: * " Am I comparing my life to hers? Do I feel stuck in my own job? If so, what steps can I take to improve it?"* ( e.g., upskilling, job hunting, or reevaluating priorities). - **Remember: context matters:** If she’s talking to *your* friends who *also* have flexible jobs ( e.g., in tech or creative fields), it’s likely fine. But if she’s with people in rigid, low-paying roles ( e.g., retail, healthcare, service industries), a simple " I know not everyone has this luxury, but I’m grateful for it" would show empathy. ### **Why This Isn’t " Jealousy"— It’s Poor Communication** Her " you’re jealous" comment was unproductive, but *your* approach was equally unproductive. **You’re not the asshole for * feeling* frustrated**— but you * are* the asshole for lashing out publicly and using accusatory language (" obnoxious," " braggy"). - **Key takeaway:** * " I’m proud of my job, but I know not everyone has it easy"* is a humble way to share. * " I can do whatever I want because I’m special"* is bragging. She’s doing the former; you’re reacting to the latter ( even if it wasn’t intentional). **Fix it:** Apologize for the public criticism, then have a calm, non-confrontational talk about *your* feelings ( not her " flaws"). Example: > * " I’m sorry I called you out at the party—that was harsh. I’m actually feeling insecure about my own job lately, and I took it out on you. I know you worked hard for this, and I’m proud of you. Can we talk about how to share these things in a way that doesn’t make others feel uncomfortable?"* **Final verdict: 1 (Yes, AITA)** for the *manner* of your response, not the underlying concern. Your intention was valid, but your execution was hurtful and counterproductive. 💬
